findings.claim: The futurebiohackers CIFAR-100 recipe reaches 75.29% (std 0.25 pp) in 8.11 s (std 0.02 s) on an A100-SXM4. It is an airbench port at 8.5 epochs with a 576-channel last block, compile and warm-up in build, and data transfer, normalisation and whitening init in timed prepare. Their note says 'Muon lost to SGD at every size', so Muon was dropped from their final recipe.
findings.relevance: This is external evidence against H1.2/H1.2.1. In E006 the Muon switch was confounded with a batch-size change from 1024 to 2000, so the +0.66 pp may come from batch size or an RNG re-draw rather than Muon. This raises the prior for the H1.2.2 ablation (SGD at batch 2000 on the E026/E027 tip) and supports testing it. Our tip, at about 5.86 s, is already about 28% faster than this external recipe.

findings.claim: The reference Muon uses steps=3 Newton-Schulz iterations, not 5. It renormalises filters every step (p.data.mul_(len(p.data)**0.5 / p.data.norm())), so filter wd is inert. Other settings: Muon lr 0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov; SGD on biases at lr 0.053 and on the head at lr 0.67, momentum 0.85; batch 2000; ceil(8*len(loader)) steps; LS 0.2; BN momentum 0.6, eps 1e-12; linear decay to 0 with no warm-up. The whitening bias trains only for the first 3 epochs (whiten_bias_grad=(step < whiten_bias_train_steps)).
findings.relevance: For H1.2.3: if the port copied 5 NS iterations, going to 3 matches the reference and costs nothing in principle. For H1.5.4: if the port renormalises the filters, filter wd is inert and E016's gain came from the SGD groups. Training the whitening bias for only 3 epochs is a built-in example of FreezeOut-style truncation (H2.6) that the port may not apply yet.

findings.claim: Hiverge (1.99 s CIFAR-10 record) trains the whitening bias for only the first 20% of steps. Its other settings: batch 1536 for 7.65 epochs, no warm-up (linear decay from step 0), Muon lr 0.205, momentum 0.655, 3 NS iterations. Filter renormalisation is progressive: norm_freq = 2 + int(15*progress), so renormalisation drops from every 2 steps to every 17. Filters get a target-magnitude schedule from 0.5012 to 0.0786 instead of wd. Remaining settings: LS 0.09, SiLU instead of GELU, BN momentum 0.5566, and brightness/contrast jitter of 0.14/0.13.
findings.relevance: Batch 1536 is evidence that a batch below 2000 is good under Muon (H5.1.2) at about 7.65 epochs. The shrinking filter-norm target is an untested alternative to wd for H1.5. Freezing the whitening bias at 20% of steps is a cheap extension of E028's freeze. SiLU is cheaper elementwise than GELU, which matters because E028 found group-1 backward memory-bound. The no-warm-up setting agrees with E029 (warm-up length flat).

findings.claim: The Lookahead update lerps every float entry of net.state_dict() toward the EMA: 'for ema_param, net_param in zip(self.net_ema.values(), net.state_dict().values()): if net_param.dtype in (torch.half, torch.float): ema_param.lerp_(net_param, 1-decay)'. That includes the BN running_mean/var buffers, not only parameters. Other details: alpha = 0.95**5 * (step/total)**3, applied every 5 steps; whiten_bias_epochs = 3 of 45; widths 128/384/512; LS 0.2; and a proxy-filtering (top-loss) step.
findings.relevance: For H1.3.5/H1.3.6: the BN running stats are averaged together with the weights, so the final stats are a mix of stats from different fast weights rather than the stats of the averaged weights. A BN recompute at 32 px on a few thousand training images is the standard fix. E025 and E030 suggest the alpha schedule is a local optimum; the BN-buffer handling is the remaining untested part.

findings.source: arxiv.org/html/2411.18704 (Exponential Moving Average of Weights in Deep Learning: Dynamics and Benefits)
findings.claim: Recomputing BN statistics for the EMA model on CIFAR-100 / ResNet-18 raised test accuracy from 78.07% to 78.55% (+0.48 pp). The authors find that parameters tolerate longer averaging windows than BN statistics, and that EMAs with the largest windows fail unless BN stats are recomputed.
findings.relevance: This directly supports the size predicted by H1.3.6 (≥0.2 pp from a BN recompute after averaging). The gain could be larger here because airbench's BN momentum of 0.6 makes the running stats depend on only the last few batches. It would be a time-neutral accuracy booster to fund E028's freeze or more epoch trims.

findings.claim: 'The biases are trained for 3 epochs, after which we disable their gradient to increase backward-pass throughput, which improves training speed without reducing accuracy.' The paper also credits Lookahead with cutting the required epochs from 18 to 12, and it fixes BN momentum at 0.6 without an ablation.
findings.relevance: Published evidence that truncating the backward pass at the stem saves time at no accuracy cost in this architecture family. It agrees with E028's −8.8% time at −0.01 pp held-out. It suggests pushing the truncation further: freeze the whitening bias earlier, and freeze group 1 from an earlier point (0.6–0.7) once the margin is rebuilt.

findings.claim: FreezeOut anneals each layer's LR to 0 with a per-layer cosine, 0.5*a0*(1+cos(pi*t/t_i)). Once a layer's LR reaches 0 it is put in inference mode and dropped from all later backward passes, and its BN no longer computes batch means and variances. The recommended default is a cubic schedule with LR scaling and t0=0.8, with linear at t0=0.5 as the alternative. Results: about 20% wall-clock saving with no accuracy loss on ResNets/WRNs (WRN40-4 on CIFAR-100 even improved at the same epochs), a 3% accuracy loss on DenseNets, and no gain on VGG.
findings.relevance: E028 kept group-1 BN in train mode. FreezeOut's practice of switching frozen layers to eval-mode BN (running stats) removes the memory-bound BN statistics work on the largest maps, which could save more time per frozen step. A staggered schedule (whitening bias, then group 1, then possibly the first conv of group 2) is the natural extension. One caution: BN in eval mode during training with BN momentum 0.6 uses noisy running stats, so a short stat recompute at the freeze point may be needed.

findings.source: arxiv.org/abs/2603.28921 (Critical Damping as a Momentum Schedule)
findings.claim: A momentum schedule mu(t)=1-2*sqrt(alpha(t)) reaches 90% on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 2.34x faster but ends 0.46 pp lower. On CIFAR-100 the accuracy cost grows to −1.7 pp, so the accuracy-matched gain shrinks to 1.14x. The paper also reports that selecting which layers to retrain by gradient attribution does no better than random across all 35 combinations.
findings.relevance: This is weak evidence that momentum-schedule tricks transfer poorly to CIFAR-100 when the endpoint matters. Momentum schedules are therefore a low-priority lever, which fits the flat scalar-tuning results (E009, E013, E014, E029).

findings.claim: Drop-Muon updates only the layers from a sampled minimum index up to the output, skipping backward through early layers on some steps. It moves the sampling probability from shallow to deep layers over training and reports up to 1.4x wall-clock speedup to equal accuracy. The experiments use only 3-layer CNNs on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-10 gains were small and measured on training accuracy.
findings.relevance: A stochastic alternative to E028's deterministic freeze: skip group-1 or whitening backward on a growing fraction of steps rather than all at once. The evidence is weak, from toy nets and training accuracy.

findings.source: arxiv.org/abs/2507.01598 (Convergence Bound and Critical Batch Size of Muon Optimizer)
findings.claim: Theory and experiments (ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, VGG-16 on CIFAR-100) find that Muon's critical batch size is smaller than AdamW's and that its data efficiency holds at large batches.
findings.relevance: Mixed support for H5/H5.1: Muon tolerates large batches, but a smaller critical batch means 2000 may already be above the optimum for a roughly 220-step run. That fits Hiverge's batch 1536 and favours testing H5.1.2 (smaller batch) before H5.1.1 or H5.1.3 (larger batch).

findings.claim: Fable's CIFAR-10 record (1.717 s legitimate, 1.828 s with gaming techniques, vs Hiverge's 1.98 s) came mainly from progressive resizing: 24 px, then 28 px after a few epochs, then 32 px, plus CUDA-graph and optimizer-fusion work and pooling changes. The gaming techniques were precomputing all augmented data in untimed setup (about 150 ms), a 60 s GPU cooldown sleep (about 9 ms), and host lottery. Opus 4.8 and GPT 5.5, working from airbench, converged on 9.0–9.75-epoch cuts.
findings.relevance: Confirms that resizing plus systems work is the main lever, as in H2.3 and H2.2. It also marks forbidden moves for this task: augmentation precompute in build would break the rule that real data stays out of build, and sleeps are banned. The 24/28/32 phase design is the same as ours, so no further resizing gains are expected from copying it.

findings.claim: The organizer's ResNet9 baseline (width 64, 40 epochs) on an A100 80GB PCIe reached 75.36% (75.56/75.16) in 59.30 s over 2 trials. On the earlier L40, over 50 trials, it gave mean 75.48% with std 0.25 pp and time std 0.14 s. The forks have no public leaderboard or other submissions.
findings.relevance: The per-seed std of about 0.25 pp at 50 trials on the official harness matches H4.1's noise model. No public competitor submission beats the tip.

structured_output.summary:
Muon's +0.66 pp in E006 may not be a Muon effect. The futurebiohackers CIFAR-100 recipe (75.29% in 8.11 s on A100-SXM4, 8.5 epochs, 576-wide last block) says Muon lost to SGD at every size and dropped it. E006 also changed batch from 1024 to 2000 at the same time, so H1.2.2 (SGD at batch 2000 on the tip) is a priority test.

The reference Muon code points to two cheap things to check in the port:
- **Newton-Schulz steps:** airbench94_muon and Hiverge both use 3, not 5 (H1.2.3).
- **Filter renormalisation:** the reference renormalises filters every step, which makes filter wd inert (H1.5.4). Hiverge renormalises progressively less often (every 2 steps rising to every 17) and replaces wd with a shrinking filter-norm target (0.5 to 0.079).

Hiverge also uses batch 1536 at 7.65 epochs, LS 0.09, no warm-up and SiLU. The batch evidence and the Muon critical-batch paper (arXiv 2507.01598) favour testing a smaller batch (H5.1.2) before a larger one.

**Averaging and BN:** airbench96_faster's Lookahead lerps every float entry of state_dict(), so the BN running stats get averaged along with the weights. The EMA-dynamics paper (arXiv 2411.18704) measured +0.48 pp on CIFAR-100 / ResNet-18 from recomputing BN stats after EMA. This supports H1.3.6 as a near-free way to win back margin.

**Backward truncation (E028):** this has outside support. airbench trains the whitening bias for only 3 epochs and then turns off its gradient "to increase backward-pass throughput … without reducing accuracy"; Hiverge stops it at 20% of steps. FreezeOut saw about 20% speedup with no loss on ResNets/WRNs, including CIFAR-100. Its recommended default is a cubic per-layer schedule with t0 = 0.8, and it puts frozen layers' BN in inference mode, which E028 did not do. Possible extensions:
- freeze the whitening bias earlier;
- freeze group 1 earlier once the margin is rebuilt;
- run frozen BN in eval mode, possibly with a stat recompute at the freeze point;
- skip early-layer backward on a random subset of steps, as Drop-Muon does (weak evidence, toy nets only).

**Lower priority:** momentum-schedule tricks (the critical-damping paper loses 1.7 pp on CIFAR-100) and more resizing ideas (Fable's CIFAR-10 record used the same 24/28/32 design). Two of Fable's gains would break this task's rules: precomputing augmentations in setup and a GPU cooldown sleep.

The organizer baseline's 50-trial std of 0.25 pp matches the H4.1 noise model, and no public CIFAR-100 submission beats the current tip.
